text: Knowing how diseases spread onto a farm or into a village helps reduce contamination risk. Sick animals spread microbes through feces and nasal discharge — close contact readily transmits virus, bacteria, fungi, or parasites to healthy animals; a particular danger is that animals still incubating a disease (the gap between exposure and first symptoms) look healthy while already shedding microbes. People spread microbes via soiled footwear (e.g. from walking through a Live Bird Market, then carrying contaminated matter home) and via hands, since warm, humid skin is a good environment for microbes picked up from touching animals or contaminated materials — hand-washing with soap is essential. Vehicles and equipment spread disease via soiled wheels carrying droppings and organic matter between farms, and via shared equipment (e.g. egg trays, feeders, drinkers) contaminated at markets or shops where many farmers gather. Pests spread disease too: insects such as mosquitoes transmit Fowl Pox, and rodents carry Salmonella and E. coli (polluting feed and water) and act as a reservoir for Leptospirosis, which affects both animals and humans. Water is a particularly important route for Bird Flu transmission — waterfowl such as ducks can look healthy while shedding large amounts of virus into ponds, where it can survive for days and contaminate other chickens or humans using that water.
